options.name: Eight used PS5 consoles
options.unit_price_note: Average sold price of a used PS5 Slim Digital over the last 30 days (424 sales) per Techfare, 2026-11-05. Typical sold range $326 to $442. Our 2026-10-17 post used a lower range of $180 to $450, so this is a price rise.
catches: Linux needs a jailbreak. The ps5-linux loader (README read 2026-11-05) now supports Phat and Slim firmware 3.00 to 7.61 and 11.00 to 13.60, and Pro 11.00 to 13.60. It does not list 8.x to 10.x, and a console cannot be downgraded. Our 2026-10-17 post said 7.61 was the limit; that is out of date.

The jailbreak is tethered: it has to be re-run after every reboot, can take several tries, and can crash the console. Newer firmware matters because 14.00 and 14.10 have no public kernel exploit and 14.20 patched a leaked one, so do not update a console you want to keep jailbreakable.

You cannot read the firmware from most used listings. Sellers who advertised a usable firmware (12.40 to 13.60) asked $530 to $600 on eBay on Oct 18, against $430 to $525 when no firmware was stated (search excerpts, asking prices).
Eight consoles each hold their own 16 GB shared with the system. It is not one 128 GB pool; llama.cpp splits layers across the network and runs at the speed of the slowest link.

Measured by someone else: two PS5s pooled over gigabit ran a 27B model at about 14 to 21 tok/s, and one console running a smaller version of the same model was as fast or faster at 19.7 to 22 (ps5-llama-cluster README, 2026-10-24, firmware 13.60). Pooling bought a larger version, vision and a 262K context, not speed. A LinkedIn post claims about 41 tok/s on a 35B model with two consoles; we could not open its repo, so that is unverified.

Warranty is void and a ban from the PlayStation network is possible; the project warns that sustained inference may overheat the console. We have not looked into the legal side of breaking the console protections. Read up before you try.

options.name: Eight AMD BC-250 boards (ex-mining, built on the PS5 chip family)
options.unit_price_note: One US eBay listing for a used ASRock BC-250 16 GB with an SSD and free shipping, US $290, listing last updated 2026-11-03 (259 sold). Other listings seen: $399.99 with shipping to some regions, 249 EUR in Germany, $329 new from Japan plus shipping. These are asking prices, and the board needs a power supply, case or frame, cooling and a network port.
options.network: 1 Gbit Ethernet per board (Tecce used gigabit; a 2.5 Gbit card is untested by us)
options.verdict: A cheap experiment, not a 128 GB machine
catches: It boots ordinary Linux, so there is no jailbreak, but it is a bare board: you supply power, cooling and a network connection, and a BIOS flash and a kernel patch are needed to unlock the full 40-unit mode. The patch silently reverts after a kernel upgrade.
Each board has 16 GB shared between the processor and the graphics side, and the setup guide says you silently get only about half of it until a kernel memory setting is raised.

Largest measured cluster we found: five boards over 2.5-gigabit Ethernet ran Qwen3.5-122B-A10B at 3-bit (a 43 GiB file) at 29.5 tok/s generating, and three boards ran a 35B mixture-of-experts model at 68 tok/s. That is the author's own production run on llama.cpp's discussion board (read, 2026-09-02). We found no eight-board result.
The three-board homelab write-up (Tecce) found two boards faster than three, one board died, and long contexts were slow. Clustering helps fit a bigger model more than it helps speed.

Passive mining heat sinks throttle in a warm room. Prices are rising and stock is thin: reports range from $150 to $220 on eBay in mid-October (Hacker News comments, excerpt) to the $290 listing above.
That the BC-250 is nearly the same silicon as a PS5 comes from a forum comment. Verify it before betting money on it.

bc250_benchmarks.caveat: One author's numbers on one board each (24 or 40 compute units unlocked), llama.cpp with Vulkan. We have not reproduced them. Ollama ran some models 32 to 44 percent slower than llama.cpp in the same guide, and a long-context test fell to 2.3 tokens per second at 64K of context.
